## Olist - Brazilian E-Commerce Marketplace

*Domain: ECOMMERCE. Source file: `backend/sql/olist/01_order_lifecycle.sql`.*

### `customer_repeat_behaviour`

Does anyone come back?

**What we found.**

This is the finding that changes what an Olist dashboard should even measure.
99,441 orders belong to 96,096 distinct people, so 1.035 orders per person. But
93,099 of those people - 96.88% - bought exactly once and never again, and only
2,997 people (3.12%) ever returned. The most orders placed by any single person
is 17.

A marketplace in which almost nobody buys twice is a fulfilment operation with
a marketplace attached. Retention, cohort lifetime value and frequency metrics
are all built on the assumption that a customer can come back; here they would
be measuring the 3.12% who did, and the honest headline is order economics,
not customer value.

_1 row(s), 87 ms._

| orders | distinct_people | orders_per_person | people_ordering_once | pct_people_ordering_once | people_ordering_twice_plus | pct_people_returning | most_orders_by_one_person |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 99441 | 96096 | 1.035 | 93099 | 96.88 | 2997 | 3.12 | 17 |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- Does anyone come back?
--
-- GROUPING IS THE WHOLE QUESTION HERE. olist.orders.customer_id is the primary
-- key of olist.customers, so it is unique BY CONSTRUCTION - one row per order.
-- Counting distinct customer_id therefore always returns the order count and
-- makes repeat purchasing impossible to see; an earlier draft of this query
-- returned exactly 1.000 orders per customer for that reason alone. The person is
-- identified by customer_unique_id, which repeats across orders.
WITH per_customer AS (
    SELECT
        c.customer_unique_id,
        count(*)                              AS orders,
        count(DISTINCT date_trunc('month', o.purchase_date)) AS active_months
    FROM olist.orders o
    JOIN olist.customers c USING (customer_id)
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT
    (SELECT count(*) FROM olist.orders)                     AS orders,
    count(*)                                                AS distinct_people,
    round((SELECT count(*) FROM olist.orders)::numeric / count(*), 3)
                                                          AS orders_per_person,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE orders = 1)                     AS people_ordering_once,
    round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE orders = 1) / count(*), 2)
                                                          AS pct_people_ordering_once,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE orders >= 2)                    AS people_ordering_twice_plus,
    round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE orders >= 2) / count(*), 2)
                                                          AS pct_people_returning,
    max(orders)                                            AS most_orders_by_one_person
FROM per_customer;
```

</details>

### `delay_distribution`

On-time deliveries are an average; the tail is what generates complaints. This buckets the delivered orders by how far past the estimate they landed.

**What we found.**

The average hides the tail that generates complaints. 1,292 delivered orders
(1.34%) were up to a day late, but 1,790 (1.86%) fall in the `8-14 days late`
band and 1,555 (1.61%) in `more than 14 days late`. The late tail is
bimodal - either you make the promise comfortably or you miss it by a long way
- and there is almost nothing in between.

_6 row(s), 20 ms._

| delay_band | orders | pct_of_delivered |
|---|---|---|
| 1. on or before estimate | 88644 | 91.89 |
| 2. up to 1 day late | 1292 | 1.34 |
| 3. 2-3 days late | 1370 | 1.42 |
| 4. 4-7 days late | 1819 | 1.89 |
| 5. 8-14 days late | 1790 | 1.86 |
| 6. more than 14 days late | 1555 | 1.61 |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- On-time deliveries are an average; the tail is what generates complaints.
-- This buckets the delivered orders by how far past the estimate they landed.
SELECT
    CASE
        WHEN delay_days <= 0    THEN '1. on or before estimate'
        WHEN delay_days <= 1    THEN '2. up to 1 day late'
        WHEN delay_days <= 3    THEN '3. 2-3 days late'
        WHEN delay_days <= 7    THEN '4. 4-7 days late'
        WHEN delay_days <= 14   THEN '5. 8-14 days late'
        ELSE                         '6. more than 14 days late'
    END                                                     AS delay_band,
    count(*)                                              AS orders,
    round(100.0 * count(*) / sum(count(*)) OVER (), 2)     AS pct_of_delivered
FROM olist.orders
WHERE is_delivered AND delay_days IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
```

</details>

### `delivery_performance`

How reliable are Olist's delivery promises? Compares what was promised against what actually happened, and separates "late" from "so late it matters". delay_days <= 0 means delivered on or before the estimate.

**What we found.**

Olist beats its own delivery promise almost every time, and by a wide margin.
88,644 of the 96,478 delivered orders (91.88%) arrived on or before the
estimate. The average delivery took 12.56 days against a promise of 23.74 days.

The honest reading is that the estimate is not a forecast, it is a ceiling. An
on-time rate of 91.88% against a promise nearly twice the actual delivery time
tells you very little about logistics performance: average `delay_days` comes
out at -11.18, negative because the typical order arrives ahead of its promise.
The single worst order was 189 days past its estimate, and that is the number
the operations team should be looking at.

_1 row(s), 30 ms._

| is_delivered | orders | on_or_before_estimate | pct_on_time | avg_delay_days | avg_delivery_days | avg_promised_days | worst_delay_days |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| True | 96478 | 88644 | 91.88 | -11.18 | 12.56 | 23.74 | 189 |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- How reliable are Olist's delivery promises? Compares what was promised against
-- what actually happened, and separates "late" from "so late it matters".
-- delay_days <= 0 means delivered on or before the estimate.
SELECT
    o.is_delivered,
    count(*)                                              AS orders,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE o.delay_days <= 0)              AS on_or_before_estimate,
    round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE o.delay_days <= 0) / count(*), 2)
                                                          AS pct_on_time,
    round(avg(o.delay_days)::numeric, 2)                  AS avg_delay_days,
    round(avg(o.delivery_days)::numeric, 2)               AS avg_delivery_days,
    round(avg(o.estimated_days)::numeric, 2)              AS avg_promised_days,
    round(max(o.delay_days)::numeric, 0)                  AS worst_delay_days
FROM olist.orders o
WHERE o.is_delivered
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1 DESC;
```

</details>

### `geography_revenue_concentration`

Where is the demand? Uses the order's own destination, not the seller's, and reports how much revenue sits in states with no geolocation mapping at all.

**What we found.**

Demand is concentrated in the south-east. `SP` alone takes 5,998,226.96 -
37.47% of all payment value - from 41,745 orders, with `RJ` on 13.39% and `MG`
on 11.70%.

This matters for a logistics question more than a marketing one: nearly two in
every five reais is delivered into one state, so any change to carrier
performance or delivery cost there moves the whole business, while a national
average hides it.

_12 row(s), 78 ms._

| destination_state | orders | revenue | pct_of_revenue |
|---|---|---|---|
| SP | 41745 | 5998226.96 | 37.47 |
| RJ | 12852 | 2144379.69 | 13.39 |
| MG | 11635 | 1872257.26 | 11.70 |
| RS | 5466 | 890898.54 | 5.57 |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- Where is the demand? Uses the order's own destination, not the seller's, and
-- reports how much revenue sits in states with no geolocation mapping at all.
SELECT
    COALESCE(c.customer_state, '(no state)')              AS destination_state,
    count(*)                                              AS orders,
    round(sum(a.payment_total), 2)                        AS revenue,
    round(100.0 * sum(a.payment_total) / sum(sum(a.payment_total)) OVER (), 2)
                                                          AS pct_of_revenue
FROM olist.orders o
JOIN olist.order_payments_agg a USING (order_id)
LEFT JOIN olist.customers c USING (customer_id)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY revenue DESC
LIMIT 12;
```

</details>

### `monthly_revenue_trend`

How did order volume and revenue move month by month across the whole period? Olist is widely described as a high-growth marketplace; the shape of this series is the first thing any dashboard should show. count(DISTINCT c.customer_unique_id), NOT customer_id: orders.customer_id is the primary key of olist.customers and is unique per order, so counting it here would report the same number of "customers" as orders in every month and make it look as though nobody ever bought twice.

**What we found.**

Olist is a growth story that runs into a wall, not one that runs off the end of
the data. Orders climb from 800 in 2017-01 to a peak of 7,544 in 2017-11,
settle into a plateau across 2018, and then fall off a cliff: 15 orders in
2018-09 and 4 in 2018-10. The dataset ends because the marketplace effectively
stopped taking orders.

Note that orders now exceed customers in every month (800 orders from 765
customers in 2017-01, for instance). That gap is repeat purchasing, and it is
the subject of the next query.

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- How did order volume and revenue move month by month across the whole period?
-- Olist is widely described as a high-growth marketplace; the shape of this
-- series is the first thing any dashboard should show.
-- count(DISTINCT c.customer_unique_id), NOT customer_id: orders.customer_id is
-- the primary key of olist.customers and is unique per order, so counting it
-- here would report the same number of "customers" as orders in every month and
-- make it look as though nobody ever bought twice.
SELECT
    to_char(date_trunc('month', o.purchase_date), 'YYYY-MM') AS month,
    count(*)                                              AS orders,
    count(DISTINCT c.customer_unique_id)                  AS customers,
    round(sum(a.payment_total), 2)                        AS revenue,
    round(avg(a.payment_total), 2)                        AS avg_order_value,
    round(sum(a.payment_count), 0)                        AS payment_rows
FROM olist.orders o
JOIN olist.order_payments_agg a USING (order_id)
JOIN olist.customers c USING (customer_id)
WHERE a.payment_total > 0
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
```

</details>

### `multi_payment_orders`

Some orders are settled by several payments. This is why order_payments_agg has fewer rows than payments, and why revenue must not be counted per row.

**What we found.**

Most orders are settled cleanly: 96,479 of them (97.02%) are closed by exactly
one payment. But 2,382 orders need two payments, and the tail is long - one
order was settled by 29 separate payments.

This is the mechanical reason the aggregate payment table has fewer rows than
the raw one, and it is why revenue must be summed from the aggregate rather
than from the payment table. Counting payment rows would double-count every
order that was settled in instalments.

_20 row(s), 11 ms._

|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 96479 | 97.02 | 15516764.17 | 160.83 |
| 2 | 2382 | 2.40 | 413304.19 | 173.51 |
| 3 | 301 | 0.30 | 38023.71 | 126.32 |
| 4 | 108 | 0.11 | 11173.30 | 103.46 |
| 5 | 52 | 0.05 | 6711.72 | 129.07 |
| 6 | 36 | 0.04 | 6690.19 | 185.84 |
| 7 | 28 | 0.03 | 6399.14 | 228.54 |
| 8 | 11 | 0.01 | 1439.89 | 130.90 |
| 9 | 9 | 0.01 | 1693.10 | 188.12 |
| 10 | 5 | 0.01 | 537.52 | 107.50 |
| 11 | 8 | 0.01 | 1301.12 | 162.64 |
| 12 | 8 | 0.01 | 1968.48 | 246.06 |
| 13 | 3 | 0.00 | 396.41 | 132.14 |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- Some orders are settled by several payments. This is why order_payments_agg
-- has fewer rows than payments, and why revenue must not be counted per row.
SELECT
    payment_count                                         AS payments_settling_order,
    count(*)                                              AS orders,
    round(100.0 * count(*) / sum(count(*)) OVER (), 2)     AS pct_of_orders,
    round(sum(payment_total), 2)                          AS revenue,
    round(avg(payment_total), 2)                          AS avg_order_value
FROM olist.order_payments_agg
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
```

</details>

### `order_status_funnel`

What actually happened to every order? Revenue is only real once an order reaches a terminal state, so this separates money that was collected from money that was attempted.

**What we found.**

Almost everything reaches a terminal state: 96,478 of the orders are
`delivered` (97.02%) and 15,422,461.77 of the payment value sits behind them
(96.34%). The statuses people worry about - `canceled` at 625 orders and
`unavailable` at 609 - are small in count but they are not small in money:
143,255.60 and 126,479.51 respectively were attempted against orders that never
completed. `invoiced` (314) and `processing` (301) are the real "in flight"
population, and a handful of orders are stuck at `created` (5) or `approved`
(2).

_8 row(s), 51 ms._

| order_status | orders | pct_of_orders | payment_attempted | pct_of_payment_attempted |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| delivered | 96478 | 97.02 | 15422461.77 | 96.34 |
| shipped | 1107 | 1.11 | 177213.96 | 1.11 |
| canceled | 625 | 0.63 | 143255.60 | 0.89 |
| unavailable | 609 | 0.61 | 126479.51 | 0.79 |
| processing | 301 | 0.30 | 69394.11 | 0.43 |
| invoiced | 314 | 0.32 | 69137.99 | 0.43 |
| created | 5 | 0.01 | 688.10 | 0.00 |
| approved | 2 | 0.00 | 241.08 | 0.00 |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- What actually happened to every order? Revenue is only real once an order
-- reaches a terminal state, so this separates money that was collected from
-- money that was attempted.
SELECT
    o.order_status,
    count(*)                                              AS orders,
    round(100.0 * count(*) / sum(count(*)) OVER (), 2)     AS pct_of_orders,
    round(sum(a.payment_total), 2)                        AS payment_attempted,
    round(100.0 * sum(a.payment_total) / sum(sum(a.payment_total)) OVER (), 2)
                                                          AS pct_of_payment_attempted
FROM olist.orders o
LEFT JOIN olist.order_payments_agg a USING (order_id)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY payment_attempted DESC NULLS LAST;
```

</details>

### `payment_behaviour`

How do customers actually pay? Installments are the interesting column: a single R$100 payment in 1 instalment and in 10 are different products.

**What we found.**

Credit cards carry 78.34% of all payment value (12,542,084.19) and boleto, the
Brazilian bank-slip method, carries 17.92%. The interesting number is inside
the card column: 51,338 card payments (66.85% of card rows) are on more than
one instalment, and those instalment payments carry 10,101,450.13 - 80.54% of
all card value. Up to 24 instalments are used.

So "credit card" is really two products: a small number of large instalment
plans and a large number of small single payments. Boleto, voucher and debit
card are always a single payment, so the instalment feature belongs to one
payment method only.

_5 row(s), 40 ms._

| payment_type | payment_rows | value | pct_of_all_value | avg_installments | max_installments | rows_on_installments | pct_rows_on_installments | value_on_installments | pct_of_type_value_on_installments |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| credit_card | 76795 | 12542084.19 | 78.34 | 3.51 | 24 | 51338 | 66.85 | 10101450.13 | 80.54 |
| boleto | 19784 | 2869361.27 | 17.92 | 1.00 | 1 | 0 | 0.00 |  |  |
| voucher | 5775 | 379436.87 | 2.37 | 1.00 | 1 | 0 | 0.00 |  |  |
| debit_card | 1529 | 217989.79 | 1.36 | 1.00 | 1 | 0 | 0.00 |  |  |
| not_defined | 3 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 1.00 | 1 | 0 | 0.00 |  |  |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- How do customers actually pay? Installments are the interesting column: a
-- single R$100 payment in 1 instalment and in 10 are different products.
SELECT
    p.payment_type,
    count(*)                                              AS payment_rows,
    round(sum(p.payment_value), 2)                        AS value,
    round(100.0 * sum(p.payment_value) / sum(sum(p.payment_value)) OVER (), 2)
                                                          AS pct_of_all_value,
    round(avg(p.payment_installments), 2)                 AS avg_installments,
    max(p.payment_installments)                           AS max_installments,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE p.payment_installments > 1)    AS rows_on_installments,
    round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE p.payment_installments > 1)
          / count(*), 2)                                  AS pct_rows_on_installments,
    round(sum(p.payment_value) FILTER (WHERE p.payment_installments > 1), 2)
                                                          AS value_on_installments,
    round(100.0 * sum(p.payment_value) FILTER (WHERE p.payment_installments > 1)
          / sum(p.payment_value), 2)                      AS pct_of_type_value_on_installments
FROM olist.payments p
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY value DESC;
```

</details>

### `review_coverage_and_score`

Only customers who were happy enough to write can be measured at all, so this reports review COVERAGE before it reports score. A 4.5 average over 6% of orders is a very different claim from a 4.5 average over 90%. DISTINCT is required, not decorative: olist.reviews holds more review rows than there are reviewed orders, so a plain count(*) over this join counts a multi-review order several times and inflates the coverage rate.

**What we found.**

Coverage first, score second, in that order. 98,673 of 99,441 orders carry a
review - 99.23%, with only 768 orders unreviewed. That is far higher than
review coverage usually is in a marketplace, and it is the precondition for
trusting any score at all: an average of 4.09 across almost every order is a
claim about the business, whereas an average over a small self-selected
minority would be a claim about the reviewers.

This query also surfaces the rejected primary key. There are 99,224 review rows
but only 98,410 distinct review_ids, so some rows reuse an id. That is recorded
as a data limitation rather than fixed, because the loader is not allowed to
delete real rows to satisfy a key.

_1 row(s), 135 ms._

| orders_total | orders_with_review | orders_without_review | pct_reviewed | avg_score_across_reviews | min_score | max_score | distinct_review_ids | review_rows |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 99441 | 98673 | 768 | 99.23 | 4.09 | 1 | 5 | 98410 | 99224 |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- Only customers who were happy enough to write can be measured at all, so this
-- reports review COVERAGE before it reports score. A 4.5 average over 6% of
-- orders is a very different claim from a 4.5 average over 90%.
-- DISTINCT is required, not decorative: olist.reviews holds more review rows
-- than there are reviewed orders, so a plain count(*) over this join counts a
-- multi-review order several times and inflates the coverage rate.
SELECT
    count(DISTINCT o.order_id)                            AS orders_total,
    count(DISTINCT o.order_id) FILTER (WHERE r.order_id IS NOT NULL)
                                                          AS orders_with_review,
    count(DISTINCT o.order_id) FILTER (WHERE r.order_id IS NULL)
                                                          AS orders_without_review,
    round(100.0 * count(DISTINCT o.order_id) FILTER (WHERE r.order_id IS NOT NULL)
          / count(DISTINCT o.order_id), 2)                AS pct_reviewed,
    round(avg(r.review_score), 2)                         AS avg_score_across_reviews,
    min(r.review_score)                                   AS min_score,
    max(r.review_score)                                   AS max_score,
    count(DISTINCT r.review_id)                           AS distinct_review_ids,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE r.review_id IS NOT NULL)       AS review_rows
FROM olist.orders o
LEFT JOIN olist.reviews r USING (order_id);
```

</details>

### `review_grain_candidates`

Which key actually holds? Tests the three plausible grains rather than asserting one. rows - distinct pairs is the surplus; zero means the key is a valid primary key.

**What we found.**

Three candidate grains, tested side by side rather than asserted:

| candidate key | surplus rows | NULL rows |
|---|---|---|
| `review_id` alone | 814 | 0 |
| `review_id` + `order_id` | 0 | 0 |
| `order_id` + `review_creation_date` | 157 | 0 |

Only the middle one holds, and it holds exactly. `order_id` with the creation
date still leaves 157 surplus rows, because one order can legitimately carry
more than one distinct review - which is a real event, not an artefact.

This is why `olist.reviews` now has a primary key rather than none. The earlier
rejection of `review_id` was our own wrong guess about the grain, not a
property of the data, so the fix was to measure the real grain rather than to
leave a keyless table behind.

_3 row(s), 394 ms._

| candidate_key | claimed_grain | surplus_rows | null_rows |
|---|---|---|---|
| review_id + order_id | 1 row per review-per-order link | 0 | 0 |
| order_id + review_creation_date | 1 row per order, repeated reviews impossible | 157 | 0 |
| review_id alone | 1 row per review | 814 | 0 |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- Which key actually holds? Tests the three plausible grains rather than
-- asserting one. rows - distinct pairs is the surplus; zero means the key is a
-- valid primary key.
SELECT 'review_id alone'   AS candidate_key, '1 row per review'        AS claimed_grain,
       count(*) - count(DISTINCT review_id) AS surplus_rows,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE review_id IS NULL) AS null_rows
FROM olist.reviews
UNION ALL
SELECT 'review_id + order_id', '1 row per review-per-order link',
       count(*) - count(DISTINCT (review_id, order_id)),
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE review_id IS NULL OR order_id IS NULL)
FROM olist.reviews
UNION ALL
SELECT 'order_id + review_creation_date', '1 row per order, repeated reviews impossible',
       count(*) - count(DISTINCT (order_id, review_creation_date)),
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE order_id IS NULL OR review_creation_date IS NULL)
FROM olist.reviews
ORDER BY surplus_rows;
```

</details>

### `review_id_forensics`

WHY review_id IS NOT A PRIMARY KEY HERE

**What we found.**

Every repeated `review_id` is one customer and one review - or, more precisely,
the dataset repeating a single review across several of that customer's
orders.

All 789 duplicated ids belong to exactly one person, carry an identical score,
identical title and message, and identical BOTH `review_creation_date` and
`review_answer_timestamp`. 764 of them appear twice and 25 appear three times,
producing 1,603 order links.

The timestamps settle it. A customer who genuinely re-submitted a review would
create a second event, and that event would carry its own creation date. There
is no second timestamp anywhere in any group, so there was only ever one review.

The chronology is the clincher. 32 of the 789 reviews name an order whose
`purchase_date` falls AFTER the review was written - 40 of the 1,603 links. A
customer cannot review an order they had not yet placed, so those associations
were manufactured rather than reported. One concrete case: a review titled
"Produto errado", carrying the lowest score on the `review_score` scale, is
attached to three orders by one customer - the first delivered before the review
was written, the other two placed after it.

Verdict: this is a one-to-many fan-out in how Olist assembled the dataset, not
customer behaviour and not corruption in transit. The honest grain is one row
per (review, order) association, which is what the schema now declares.

_3 row(s), 142 ms._

| rows_in_group | review_ids | all_one_person | all_same_score | all_same_text | all_same_both_timestamps | impossible_chronology | order_links | impossible_order_links |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 764 | 764 | 764 | 764 | 764 | 26 | 1528 | 28 |
| 3 | 25 | 25 | 25 | 25 | 25 | 6 | 75 | 12 |
|  | 789 | 789 | 789 | 789 | 789 | 32 | 1603 | 40 |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- WHY review_id IS NOT A PRIMARY KEY HERE
--
-- review_id repeats: 99,224 rows carry only 98,410 distinct values. The obvious
-- reading is that a customer re-submitted the same review, but the evidence says
-- something else entirely. This query lays out the test, one row per duplicated
-- review_id.
--
-- The discriminator is the timestamp. A genuine re-submission is a second event
-- and would carry its own creation and answer times. If every duplicated row
-- shares both timestamps exactly, there was only ever ONE review, and the
-- dataset is repeating it across several of that customer's orders.
--
-- The second column, orders_placed_after_the_review, is the clincher. A customer
-- cannot review an order they had not yet placed, so any row where it happens
-- proves the association was manufactured rather than reported.
WITH duplicated AS (
    SELECT review_id, count(*) AS rows_in_group
    FROM olist.reviews
    GROUP BY 1
    HAVING count(*) > 1
),
per_review AS (
    SELECT
        r.review_id,
        max(d.rows_in_group)                                    AS rows_in_group,
        count(DISTINCT r.order_id)                               AS distinct_orders,
        count(DISTINCT c.customer_unique_id)                     AS distinct_people,
        count(DISTINCT r.review_score)                           AS distinct_scores,
        -- coalesce matters: most reviews carry no title at all, and
        -- count(DISTINCT review_comment_title) ignores NULLs, so it would
        -- report 0 distinct titles for a group and make "all the same" look
        -- false when it is merely absent.
        count(DISTINCT coalesce(r.review_comment_title, '<none>'))   AS distinct_titles,
        count(DISTINCT coalesce(r.review_comment_message, '<none>')) AS distinct_messages,
        count(DISTINCT r.review_creation_date)                   AS distinct_creation_dates,
        count(DISTINCT r.review_answer_timestamp)                AS distinct_answer_dates,
        count(*) FILTER (WHERE o.purchase_date > r.review_creation_date)
                                                               AS orders_placed_after_the_review,
        count(DISTINCT o.customer_id)                            AS customer_rows_behind_the_orders
    FROM olist.reviews r
    JOIN duplicated d ON d.review_id = r.review_id
    JOIN olist.orders o    ON o.order_id = r.order_id
    JOIN olist.customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT
    rows_in_group,
    count(*)                                                     AS review_ids,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE distinct_people = 1)                  AS all_one_person,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE distinct_scores = 1)                  AS all_same_score,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE distinct_titles = 1 AND distinct_messages = 1)
                                                                 AS all_same_text,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE distinct_creation_dates = 1 AND distinct_answer_dates = 1)
                                                                 AS all_same_both_timestamps,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE orders_placed_after_the_review > 0)   AS impossible_chronology,
    sum(distinct_orders)                                         AS order_links,
    sum(orders_placed_after_the_review)                          AS impossible_order_links
FROM per_review
-- GROUPING SETS adds an "all" row so the totals are measured rather than
-- summed by hand in the write-up.
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((rows_in_group), ())
ORDER BY rows_in_group NULLS LAST;
```

</details>

### `review_score_distribution`

Score distribution alongside the comment volume behind each score. A 1-star with no comment is a different event from a 1-star with a paragraph.

**What we found.**

The distribution is heavily top-weighted: 57,328 five-star reviews (57.78%)
against 11,424 one-star reviews (11.51%).

The more useful signal is the comment column, and it runs opposite to the
score. 76.55% of one-star reviewers left a comment, compared with 31.22% of
four-star reviewers, and the average one-star comment runs to 100 characters
against 52 for a five-star. Dissatisfaction is expressed; satisfaction is
silent. Any sentiment model trained on review TEXT will therefore be trained
overwhelmingly on the minority of unhappy customers, which is a sampling
problem in the data and not something the model can fix.

_5 row(s), 17 ms._

| review_score | reviews | pct_of_reviews | pct_with_comment | avg_comment_chars |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 11424 | 11.51 | 76.55 | 100 |
| 2 | 3151 | 3.18 | 68.07 | 97 |
| 3 | 8179 | 8.24 | 43.49 | 83 |
| 4 | 19142 | 19.29 | 31.22 | 62 |
| 5 | 57328 | 57.78 | 35.85 | 52 |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- Score distribution alongside the comment volume behind each score. A 1-star
-- with no comment is a different event from a 1-star with a paragraph.
SELECT
    r.review_score,
    count(*)                                              AS reviews,
    round(100.0 * count(*) / sum(count(*)) OVER (), 2)     AS pct_of_reviews,
    round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE r.review_comment_message IS NOT NULL)
          / count(*), 2)                                  AS pct_with_comment,
    round(avg(length(r.review_comment_message)), 0)       AS avg_comment_chars
FROM olist.reviews r
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
```

</details>

### `seller_concentration`

How dependent is the marketplace on its biggest sellers? This measures gross merchandise value as the SUM OF order_items.item_total, NOT the order's payment_total: an order with six items has six rows, so joining items to payments and summing the order total would count that order's revenue six times. Each item belongs to exactly one seller, so item-level GMV cannot double-count. WITH seller_gmv AS (

**What we found.**

The marketplace is extremely long-tailed. The top 100 sellers are 3.23% of the
3,095 sellers and take 44.37% of gross merchandise value. The top 1,000 (32.31%
of sellers) take 91.06%, leaving the remaining sellers to share the rest.

Two consequences follow. Any seller-level forecast or recommendation has to
handle a power law, not a normal distribution. And marketplace-wide averages
describe a minority of the supply base: the top seller alone carries 249,640.70
across 1,132 orders, more than three times what a median seller will ever see.

_7 row(s), 121 ms._

| top_n_sellers | pct_of_sellers | sellers_cumulative | seller_order_pairs | gmv_cumulative | pct_of_gmv |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.03 | 1 | 1132 | 249640.70 | 1.58 |
| 10 | 0.32 | 10 | 9875 | 2028716.63 | 12.80 |
| 50 | 1.62 | 50 | 29021 | 5108502.07 | 32.24 |
| 100 | 3.23 | 100 | 40648 | 7030376.15 | 44.37 |
| 500 | 16.16 | 500 | 73047 | 12267116.70 | 77.43 |
| 1000 | 32.31 | 1000 | 88302 | 14427117.55 | 91.06 |
| 3095 | 100.00 | 3095 | 100010 | 15843553.24 | 100.00 |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- How dependent is the marketplace on its biggest sellers? This measures gross
-- merchandise value as the SUM OF order_items.item_total, NOT the order's
-- payment_total: an order with six items has six rows, so joining items to
-- payments and summing the order total would count that order's revenue six
-- times. Each item belongs to exactly one seller, so item-level GMV cannot
-- double-count.
WITH seller_gmv AS (
    SELECT
        i.seller_id,
        count(DISTINCT i.order_id) AS orders,
        sum(i.item_total)          AS gmv
    FROM olist.order_items i
    GROUP BY 1
),
ranked AS (
    SELECT
        row_number() OVER (ORDER BY gmv DESC) AS seller_rank,
        orders,
        gmv
    FROM seller_gmv
),
thresholds(n) AS (VALUES (1), (10), (50), (100), (500), (1000), (3095))
SELECT
    t.n                                                   AS top_n_sellers,
    round(100.0 * t.n / (SELECT count(*) FROM seller_gmv), 2) AS pct_of_sellers,
    count(*)                                              AS sellers_cumulative,
    -- An order with items from three sellers is counted once per seller, so this
    -- is (seller, order) pairs, not distinct orders.
    sum(r.orders)                                         AS seller_order_pairs,
    round(sum(r.gmv), 2)                                  AS gmv_cumulative,
    round(100.0 * sum(r.gmv) / (SELECT sum(gmv) FROM seller_gmv), 2)
                                                          AS pct_of_gmv
FROM thresholds t
JOIN ranked r ON r.seller_rank <= t.n
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1;
```

</details>

## DataCo - Supply Chain Dataset

*Domain: SUPPLY CHAIN. Source file: `backend/sql/dataco/01_supply_chain_performance.sql`.*

### `customer_segments`

Consumer, Corporate and Home Office are DataCo's three segments. Segment value per order and per customer is the comparison that matters.

**What we found.**

The three segments are almost interchangeable. Margin runs 10.86% (Consumer),
10.77% (Corporate) and 10.59% (Home Office); sales per customer run 1,785.49,
1,790.10 and 1,753.78. Consumer is the largest at 34,119 orders, but it is not
more profitable per unit of business, and Corporate is not worth a different
operating model.

_3 row(s), 357 ms._

| segment | customers | orders | sales | profit | margin_pct | avg_order_sales | sales_per_customer |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Consumer | 10695 | 34119 | 19095789.79 | 2073487.67 | 10.86 | 559.68 | 1785.49 |
| Corporate | 6239 | 19856 | 11168406.63 | 1202574.96 | 10.77 | 562.47 | 1790.10 |
| Home Office | 3718 | 11777 | 6520537.89 | 690840.34 | 10.59 | 553.67 | 1753.78 |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- Consumer, Corporate and Home Office are DataCo's three segments. Segment
-- value per order and per customer is the comparison that matters.
SELECT
    c.customer_segment                                       AS segment,
    count(DISTINCT c.customer_id)                           AS customers,
    count(DISTINCT o.order_id)                               AS orders,
    round(sum(o.order_sales), 2)                             AS sales,
    round(sum(o.order_profit), 2)                            AS profit,
    round(100.0 * sum(o.order_profit) / sum(o.order_sales), 2) AS margin_pct,
    round(sum(o.order_sales) / count(DISTINCT o.order_id), 2) AS avg_order_sales,
    round(sum(o.order_sales) / count(DISTINCT c.customer_id), 2) AS sales_per_customer
FROM dataco.orders o
JOIN dataco.customers c USING (customer_id)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY sales DESC;
```

</details>

### `discount_vs_margin`

Does discounting actually pay? Buckets order lines by the discount they carried so the relationship can be read without assuming one exists.

**What we found.**

Discounting costs margin, monotonically and almost linearly. Lines with no
discount return 13.09%. The `1-14% off` band returns 11.22%, `15-19% off`
returns 9.88%, and the deepest band present, `20-29% off`, returns 9.03%.

The final two buckets of the query - `30-49% off` and `50%+ off` - are empty.
That matters: this data can tell you the cost of discounting down to the
deepest band it actually contains, and can say nothing at all about what
happens past it. An extrapolation beyond the observed range would be invention.

_4 row(s), 229 ms._

| discount_band | order_lines | avg_discount_rate | sales | profit | margin_pct | avg_profit_ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. no discount | 10028 | 0.0000 | 2042369.14 | 267412.40 | 13.09 | 0.1275 |
| 2. 1-14% off | 110317 | 0.0655 | 22477269.92 | 2522354.86 | 11.22 | 0.1212 |
| 3. 15-19% off | 40116 | 0.1650 | 8176530.70 | 807926.25 | 9.88 | 0.1179 |
| 4. 20-29% off | 20058 | 0.2250 | 4088564.55 | 369209.46 | 9.03 | 0.1197 |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- Does discounting actually pay? Buckets order lines by the discount they
-- carried so the relationship can be read without assuming one exists.
SELECT
    CASE
        WHEN order_item_discount_rate <= 0.00 THEN '1. no discount'
        WHEN order_item_discount_rate <  0.15 THEN '2. 1-14% off'
        WHEN order_item_discount_rate <  0.20 THEN '3. 15-19% off'
        WHEN order_item_discount_rate <  0.30 THEN '4. 20-29% off'
        WHEN order_item_discount_rate <  0.50 THEN '5. 30-49% off'
        ELSE                              '6. 50%+ off'
    END                                                      AS discount_band,
    count(*)                                                 AS order_lines,
    round(avg(order_item_discount_rate), 4)                 AS avg_discount_rate,
    round(sum(sales), 2)                                     AS sales,
    round(sum(order_profit_per_order), 2)                    AS profit,
    round(100.0 * sum(order_profit_per_order) / sum(sales), 2) AS margin_pct,
    round(avg(order_item_profit_ratio), 4)                  AS avg_profit_ratio
FROM dataco.order_items
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
```

</details>

### `loss_making_orders`

Orders that lost money outright. If an operations review only looks at totals these disappear inside an average; counting them makes them arguable.

**What we found.**

78.85% of orders (51,844) are profitable or break even, but the three loss
bands are not trivial: 6,628 orders sit in `small loss (0 to -100)`, 6,069 in
`moderate loss (-100 to -500)` and 1,211 in `large loss (below -500)`. The
single worst order lost -4,325.85.

Roughly one order in five loses money, which disappears entirely inside a
blended margin and is exactly the kind of thing an operations review should be
able to list.

_4 row(s), 166 ms._

| profit_band | orders | pct_of_orders | sales | profit | worst_single_order |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. profitable or break-even | 51844 | 78.85 | 28695834.71 | 6582106.76 | 0.0000 |
| 2. small loss (0 to -100) | 6628 | 10.08 | 3076257.40 | -266394.49 | -99.9500 |
| 3. moderate loss (-100 to -500) | 6069 | 9.23 | 3978527.62 | -1434448.42 | -499.1200 |
| 4. large loss (below -500) | 1211 | 1.84 | 1034114.58 | -914360.88 | -4325.8500 |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- Orders that lost money outright. If an operations review only looks at totals
-- these disappear inside an average; counting them makes them arguable.
SELECT
    CASE
        WHEN order_profit >= 0    THEN '1. profitable or break-even'
        WHEN order_profit > -100  THEN '2. small loss (0 to -100)'
        WHEN order_profit > -500  THEN '3. moderate loss (-100 to -500)'
        ELSE                           '4. large loss (below -500)'
    END                                                      AS profit_band,
    count(*)                                                 AS orders,
    round(100.0 * count(*) / sum(count(*)) OVER (), 2)      AS pct_of_orders,
    round(sum(order_sales), 2)                               AS sales,
    round(sum(order_profit), 2)                              AS profit,
    min(order_profit)                                        AS worst_single_order
FROM dataco.orders
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
```

</details>

### `margin_by_department`

The central profitability question. DataCo is widely reported to be close to break-even overall; this shows whether that is uniform or hides a mix shift.

**What we found.**

Margins are thin but not negative, and remarkably tight together: they run from
7.02% in Book Shop to 11.72% in Fitness, with the volume leader `Fan Shop` at
10.72% on 17,113,870.54 of sales.

The striking column is the discount rate, which sits inside a band of just over
a tenth of a percent in every single department - from 10.05% to 10.20%. A real
retailer does not discount eleven departments to within that margin of each
other. This is a characteristic of how the dataset was built, and it means
department-level discounting analysis has nothing to find here.

_11 row(s), 468 ms._

| department | products | order_lines | sales | profit | margin_pct | discount_given | discount_pct |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fan Shop | 9 | 66861 | 17113870.54 | 1834155.43 | 10.72 | 1735317.51 | 10.14 |
| Apparel | 8 | 48998 | 7976255.08 | 881882.93 | 11.06 | 808607.94 | 10.14 |
| Golf | 8 | 33220 | 4609028.22 | 497523.56 | 10.79 | 466929.79 | 10.13 |
| Footwear | 15 | 14525 | 4006498.77 | 410222.50 | 10.24 | 407033.10 | 10.16 |
| Outdoors | 53 | 9686 | 1253351.44 | 145251.46 | 11.59 | 127400.13 | 10.16 |
| Technology | 3 | 1465 | 1039598.96 | 113170.01 | 10.89 | 105769.72 | 10.17 |
| Fitness | 15 | 2479 | 397050.89 | 46538.06 | 11.72 | 39893.63 | 10.05 |
| Discs Shop | 4 | 2026 | 228887.73 | 24193.12 | 10.57 | 23213.73 | 10.14 |
| Health and Beauty  | 1 | 362 | 106080.48 | 9493.63 | 8.95 | 10722.37 | 10.11 |
| Pet Shop | 1 | 492 | 41524.80 | 3589.26 | 8.64 | 4206.50 | 10.13 |
| Book Shop | 1 | 405 | 12587.40 | 883.01 | 7.02 | 1283.98 | 10.20 |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- The central profitability question. DataCo is widely reported to be close to
-- break-even overall; this shows whether that is uniform or hides a mix shift.
SELECT
    p.department_name                                        AS department,
    count(DISTINCT p.product_card_id)                        AS products,
    count(*)                                                 AS order_lines,
    round(sum(i.sales), 2)                                   AS sales,
    round(sum(i.order_profit_per_order), 2)                  AS profit,
    round(100.0 * sum(i.order_profit_per_order) / sum(i.sales), 2) AS margin_pct,
    round(sum(i.order_item_discount), 2)                     AS discount_given,
    round(100.0 * sum(i.order_item_discount) / sum(i.sales), 2) AS discount_pct
FROM dataco.order_items i
JOIN dataco.products p USING (product_card_id)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY sales DESC;
```

</details>

### `order_flow_by_month`

How did order volume and value move month by month? DataCo is a 2-year window, so this shows both the level and whether the business was growing.

**What we found.**

The order count rises over the window, from 1,787 orders in 2015-01 to 2,055 in
2017-11, but sales fall from 1,051,590.06 to 626,914.37. The reconciliation is
basket size: average units per order collapse from 6.63 to 1.00.

By the end of the dataset every order contains exactly one unit. Whatever
DataCo was doing early on - bulk or multi-line orders - has stopped, and any
per-order metric that mixes the two periods is comparing two different
businesses.

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- How did order volume and value move month by month? DataCo is a 2-year
-- window, so this shows both the level and whether the business was growing.
SELECT
    to_char(date_trunc('month', order_date), 'YYYY-MM')     AS month,
    count(*)                                                 AS orders,
    count(DISTINCT customer_id)                              AS customers,
    round(sum(order_value), 2)                               AS order_value,
    round(sum(order_sales), 2)                               AS order_sales,
    round(sum(order_profit), 2)                              AS profit,
    round(100.0 * sum(order_profit) / sum(order_sales), 2)   AS margin_pct,
    round(avg(total_quantity), 2)                            AS avg_units_per_order
FROM dataco.orders
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
```

</details>

### `order_status_mix`

Not every order completed, and the ones that did not are where the money quietly disappears. Reports value by terminal status.

**What we found.**

Late delivery is the default state rather than the exception: 12,521 orders
(19.04%) are `COMPLETE` and late, against 5,174 (7.87%) shipped in advance and
4,021 (6.12%) shipped on time.

The suspicious column is margin. Every status shows a margin in the same narrow
range - including `SUSPECTED_FRAUD` orders at 10.31% and `CANCELED` orders at
10.12%, against 10.70% for the large `COMPLETE` late group. Real cancelled and
suspected-fraud orders should not carry the same profitability as fulfilled
ones, so `order_profit` in this dataset is close to a fixed percentage of sales
rather than a measured outcome. Treat it as a derived column, not as evidence.

_23 row(s), 57 ms._

| order_status | delivery_status | orders | pct_of_orders | sales | profit | margin_pct |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| COMPLETE | Late delivery | 12521 | 19.04 | 6926002.64 | 741421.11 | 10.70 |
| PENDING_PAYMENT | Late delivery | 8256 | 12.56 | 4650655.80 | 461717.83 | 9.93 |
| COMPLETE | Advance shipping | 5174 | 7.87 | 2899972.54 | 318714.58 | 10.99 |
| PROCESSING | Late delivery | 4494 | 6.83 | 2576403.71 | 282905.86 | 10.98 |
| PENDING | Late delivery | 4215 | 6.41 | 2384837.64 | 251303.90 | 10.54 |
| CLOSED | Late delivery | 4112 | 6.25 | 2270264.71 | 267919.62 | 11.80 |
| COMPLETE | Shipping on time | 4021 | 6.12 | 2269339.54 | 261600.06 | 11.53 |
| PENDING_PAYMENT | Advance shipping | 3421 | 5.20 | 1950934.31 | 220621.67 | 11.31 |
| PENDING_PAYMENT | Shipping on time | 2705 | 4.11 | 1505107.29 | 161470.74 | 10.73 |
| ON_HOLD | Late delivery | 2045 | 3.11 | 1098838.65 | 109625.95 | 9.98 |
| PROCESSING | Advance shipping | 1941 | 2.95 | 1107448.21 | 130195.41 | 11.76 |
| PENDING | Advance shipping | 1797 | 2.73 | 996486.91 | 101997.43 | 10.24 |
| CLOSED | Advance shipping | 1777 | 2.70 | 982549.75 | 104356.00 | 10.62 |
| SUSPECTED_FRAUD | Shipping canceled | 1488 | 2.26 | 825934.94 | 85136.71 | 10.31 |
| _... 9 further rows not shown ..._ | | | | | | |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- Not every order completed, and the ones that did not are where the money
-- quietly disappears. Reports value by terminal status.
SELECT
    order_status,
    delivery_status,
    count(*)                                                 AS orders,
    round(100.0 * count(*) / sum(count(*)) OVER (), 2)      AS pct_of_orders,
    round(sum(order_sales), 2)                               AS sales,
    round(sum(order_profit), 2)                              AS profit,
    round(100.0 * sum(order_profit) / sum(order_sales), 2)  AS margin_pct
FROM dataco.orders
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY orders DESC;
```

</details>

### `revenue_by_market`

DataCo is a multinational. Market share shows how concentrated the operation is geographically before any per-country drill-down.

**What we found.**

Europe is the largest market at 29.56% of sales, followed by LATAM at 27.94%
and Pacific Asia at 22.49%, with USCA at 13.77% and Africa at 6.24%.

The operational columns are flat to a degree that should be suspicious: the
late rate is between 54.13% and 55.30% in all five markets and average delay
between 0.55 and 0.58 days. Geography has no measurable effect on delivery
performance in this dataset, which means either the effect is genuinely
negligible or the shipping fields were assigned independently of the market.
Either way it is not a finding about the business.

_5 row(s), 226 ms._

| market | regions | countries | orders | sales | pct_of_sales | avg_delay_days | pct_late |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Europe | 4 | 37 | 18561 | 10872396.60 | 29.56 | 0.57 | 54.95 |
| LATAM | 3 | 29 | 17181 | 10277612.64 | 27.94 | 0.56 | 54.36 |
| Pacific Asia | 6 | 47 | 17577 | 8273743.58 | 22.49 | 0.58 | 55.30 |
| USCA | 5 | 2 | 8579 | 5066528.61 | 13.77 | 0.57 | 54.83 |
| Africa | 5 | 49 | 3854 | 2294452.88 | 6.24 | 0.55 | 54.13 |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- DataCo is a multinational. Market share shows how concentrated the operation
-- is geographically before any per-country drill-down.
SELECT
    market,
    count(DISTINCT order_region)                             AS regions,
    count(DISTINCT order_country)                            AS countries,
    count(*)                                                 AS orders,
    round(sum(order_sales), 2)                               AS sales,
    round(100.0 * sum(order_sales) / sum(sum(order_sales)) OVER (), 2)
                                                              AS pct_of_sales,
    round(avg(shipping_delay_days), 2)                       AS avg_delay_days,
    round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE is_late) / count(*), 2) AS pct_late
FROM dataco.orders
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY sales DESC;
```

</details>

### `shipping_performance`

DataCo publishes a promise (days_for_shipment_scheduled) and an outcome (days_for_shipping_real). This measures the gap, by shipping mode.

**What we found.**

Read the late rate backwards. `First Class` is "late" on 95.27% of orders, but
the average delay is exactly 1.00 day, because the promise was 1.00 day.
`Second Class` is late 76.72% of the time with an average 2.00-day delay against
a 2.00-day promise. `Standard Class` is late only 38.13% of the time and its
average delay is 0.00 days.

So the metric tracks how tight the promise is, not whether the operation
failed. Nobody should build a carrier scorecard on `is_late` without also
looking at the magnitude of the delay.

_4 row(s), 63 ms._

| shipping_mode | orders | pct_late | avg_days_promised | avg_days_actual | avg_delay_days | avg_lead_time_days | worst_delay_days |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Standard Class | 39324 | 38.13 | 4.00 | 4.00 | 0.00 | 4.00 | 2 |
| Second Class | 12778 | 76.72 | 2.00 | 4.00 | 2.00 | 4.00 | 4 |
| First Class | 10079 | 95.27 | 1.00 | 2.00 | 1.00 | 2.00 | 1 |
| Same Day | 3571 | 46.15 | 0.00 | 0.48 | 0.48 | 0.50 | 1 |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- DataCo publishes a promise (days_for_shipment_scheduled) and an outcome
-- (days_for_shipping_real). This measures the gap, by shipping mode.
SELECT
    shipping_mode,
    count(*)                                                 AS orders,
    round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE is_late) / count(*), 2) AS pct_late,
    round(avg(days_for_shipment_scheduled), 2)              AS avg_days_promised,
    round(avg(days_for_shipping_real), 2)                   AS avg_days_actual,
    round(avg(shipping_delay_days), 2)                      AS avg_delay_days,
    round(avg(lead_time_days)::numeric, 2)                  AS avg_lead_time_days,
    max(shipping_delay_days)                                 AS worst_delay_days
FROM dataco.orders
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY orders DESC;
```

</details>

### `worst_categories_by_margin`

The bottom of the margin table. A category can be high-volume and still lose money on every unit, which no revenue ranking would reveal.

**What we found.**

The bottom of the margin table is where the money is being lost.
`Strength Training` sells 54,895.53 and keeps 0.61% - 18 of its order lines
lose money outright. `As Seen on  TV!` is at 3.47% and `Men's Clothing` at
4.57%.

Volume matters too: `Shop By Sport` has 10,984 order lines and loses money on
2,154 of them at a 9.91% margin, and `Video Games` loses on 181 lines. A category
ranking by revenue would show none of this.

_12 row(s), 492 ms._

| category | department | products | order_lines | sales | profit | margin_pct | lines_losing_money |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Strength Training | Footwear | 3 | 111 | 54895.53 | 332.31 | 0.61 | 18 |
| As Seen on  TV! | Footwear | 1 | 68 | 20597.94 | 714.43 | 3.47 | 14 |
| Men's Clothing | Apparel | 1 | 208 | 43856.80 | 2006.04 | 4.57 | 50 |
| Basketball | Fitness | 3 | 67 | 27099.33 | 1845.67 | 6.81 | 11 |
| Books  | Book Shop | 1 | 405 | 12587.40 | 883.01 | 7.02 | 78 |
| Video Games | Discs Shop | 1 | 838 | 33310.50 | 2717.52 | 8.16 | 181 |
| DVDs | Discs Shop | 1 | 483 | 79395.54 | 6655.43 | 8.38 | 102 |
| Pet Supplies | Pet Shop | 1 | 492 | 41524.80 | 3589.26 | 8.64 | 104 |
| Health and Beauty | Health and Beauty  | 1 | 362 | 106080.48 | 9493.63 | 8.95 | 85 |
| Kids' Golf Clubs | Outdoors | 8 | 384 | 98797.58 | 9045.84 | 9.16 | 77 |
| Shop By Sport | Golf | 3 | 10984 | 1309522.02 | 129813.96 | 9.91 | 2154 |
| Golf Apparel | Outdoors | 3 | 441 | 34969.75 | 3496.31 | 10.00 | 88 |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- The bottom of the margin table. A category can be high-volume and still lose
-- money on every unit, which no revenue ranking would reveal.
SELECT
    p.category_name                                          AS category,
    p.department_name                                        AS department,
    count(DISTINCT p.product_card_id)                        AS products,
    count(*)                                                 AS order_lines,
    round(sum(i.sales), 2)                                   AS sales,
    round(sum(i.order_profit_per_order), 2)                  AS profit,
    round(100.0 * sum(i.order_profit_per_order) / sum(i.sales), 2) AS margin_pct,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE i.order_profit_per_order < 0)     AS lines_losing_money
FROM dataco.order_items i
JOIN dataco.products p USING (product_card_id)
GROUP BY 1, 2
HAVING sum(i.sales) > 0
ORDER BY margin_pct ASC
LIMIT 12;
```

</details>

## Dunn & Bradstreet Complete Journey

*Domain: CPG / RETAIL. Source file: `backend/sql/dunnhumby/01_household_behaviour.sql`.*

### `campaign_performance`

Dunn & Bradstreet ran 30 named campaigns. The control group matters: comparing contacted households against the panel AVERAGE is not a control at all, because campaigns were aimed at frequent shoppers, so the contacted group is pre-loaded with high spenders. This compares each campaign's contacted households against the households that were NEVER contacted by anything. WITH household_spend AS (

**What we found.**

Contacted households average 5,176.36 in spend against 1,028.54 for households
never contacted by any campaign - a gap of 4,147.82 on the largest campaign.

That gap is selection, not effect. Campaigns were aimed at the panel's heaviest
shoppers, so comparing contacted households against anyone else measures who
was targeted. An earlier draft of this query compared against the panel average
and reported an enormous "lift", which was simply the targeting rule restated.
Nothing here identifies a causal campaign effect; that would need a holdout
group this panel does not contain.

_30 row(s), 413 ms._

| campaign | campaign_name | duration_days | households_contacted | avg_spend_contacted | avg_spend_never_contacted | lift_vs_never_contacted |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 18 | TypeA | 55 | 1133 | 5176.36 | 1028.54 | 4147.82 |
| 13 | TypeA | 47 | 1077 | 5358.69 | 1028.54 | 4330.14 |
| 8 | TypeA | 48 | 1076 | 5065.87 | 1028.54 | 4037.32 |
| 30 | TypeA | 46 | 361 | 5046.98 | 1028.54 | 4018.44 |
| 26 | TypeA | 40 | 332 | 5044.75 | 1028.54 | 4016.20 |
| 22 | TypeB | 32 | 276 | 7373.73 | 1028.54 | 6345.18 |
| 20 | TypeC | 70 | 244 | 7625.68 | 1028.54 | 6597.13 |
| 14 | TypeC | 65 | 224 | 7746.40 | 1028.54 | 6717.86 |
| 11 | TypeB | 46 | 214 | 7028.92 | 1028.54 | 6000.38 |
| 17 | TypeB | 32 | 202 | 7069.39 | 1028.54 | 6040.85 |
| 7 | TypeB | 34 | 198 | 6428.12 | 1028.54 | 5399.58 |
| 16 | TypeB | 32 | 188 | 7630.04 | 1028.54 | 6601.50 |
| 25 | TypeB | 32 | 187 | 8813.35 | 1028.54 | 7784.81 |
| 23 | TypeB | 38 | 183 | 8429.33 | 1028.54 | 7400.79 |
| _... 16 further rows not shown ..._ | | | | | | |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- Dunn & Bradstreet ran 30 named campaigns. The control group matters: comparing
-- contacted households against the panel AVERAGE is not a control at all, because
-- campaigns were aimed at frequent shoppers, so the contacted group is pre-loaded
-- with high spenders. This compares each campaign's contacted households against
-- the households that were NEVER contacted by anything.
WITH household_spend AS (
    SELECT household_key, sum(sales_value) AS spend
    FROM dunnhumby.transactions
    GROUP BY 1
),
ever_contacted AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT household_key FROM dunnhumby.campaign_contacts
),
control AS (
    SELECT avg(spend) AS avg_control_spend, count(*) AS control_households
    FROM household_spend h
    WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ever_contacted e WHERE e.household_key = h.household_key)
)
SELECT
    c.campaign,
    c.description                                            AS campaign_name,
    (c.end_day - c.start_day)                                AS duration_days,
    count(DISTINCT cc.household_key)                         AS households_contacted,
    round(avg(h.spend), 2)                                   AS avg_spend_contacted,
    (SELECT round(avg_control_spend, 2) FROM control)        AS avg_spend_never_contacted,
    round(avg(h.spend) - (SELECT avg_control_spend FROM control), 2)
                                                           AS lift_vs_never_contacted
FROM dunnhumby.campaigns c
JOIN dunnhumby.campaign_contacts cc ON cc.campaign = c.campaign
JOIN household_spend h ON h.household_key = cc.household_key
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
ORDER BY households_contacted DESC;
```

</details>

### `coupon_redemption`

Coupons were sent far more often than they were redeemed. The gap between coupons issued and redemptions is the redemption rate that actually matters.

**What we found.**

1,135 distinct coupons were issued across 119,384 product/campaign rows, and
556 of them were ever redeemed - 48.99%. Those redemptions come to 2,318 rows
across 2,229 households.

Just under half of all coupons ever got used. The interesting ratio is not
redemption rate but reach: a coupon is attached to many products and campaigns,
so "did this coupon work" cannot be answered per coupon without also asking
which of those product/campaign rows it was redeemed against.

_1 row(s), 50 ms._

| coupons_defined | coupons_ever_redeemed | pct_of_coupons_redeemed | redemption_rows | households_redeeming | product_campaign_rows_issued |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1135 | 556 | 48.99 | 2318 | 2229 | 119384 |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- Coupons were sent far more often than they were redeemed. The gap between
-- coupons issued and redemptions is the redemption rate that actually matters.
--
-- coupons has 119,384 rows over only 1,135 distinct coupon_upc values, so
-- joining it to the 2,318 redemption rows on coupon_upc alone multiplies the
-- two together and reports millions of redemptions that never happened. Each
-- side is therefore aggregated to coupon_upc BEFORE the join.
WITH issued AS (
    SELECT
        coupon_upc,
        count(*)                       AS product_campaign_rows,
        count(DISTINCT campaign)       AS campaigns,
        count(DISTINCT product_id)     AS products
    FROM dunnhumby.coupons
    GROUP BY 1
),
redeemed AS (
    SELECT
        coupon_upc,
        count(*)                       AS redemption_rows,
        count(DISTINCT household_key)  AS households_redeeming
    FROM dunnhumby.coupon_redemptions
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT
    count(*)                                                  AS coupons_defined,
    count(r.coupon_upc)                                       AS coupons_ever_redeemed,
    round(100.0 * count(r.coupon_upc) / count(*), 2)          AS pct_of_coupons_redeemed,
    COALESCE(sum(r.redemption_rows), 0)                       AS redemption_rows,
    COALESCE(sum(r.households_redeeming), 0)                  AS households_redeeming,
    sum(issued.product_campaign_rows)                         AS product_campaign_rows_issued
FROM issued
LEFT JOIN redeemed r USING (coupon_upc);
```

</details>

### `demographic_coverage_gap`

The headline data-quality finding for this source. transaction_data.csv names 2,500 distinct households; hh_demographic.csv names only 801, and the file is byte-identical to the copy inside the publisher's own zip, so this is the publisher's coverage and not a truncated download. Any demographic split is therefore a minority-sample split and has to be described as one.

**What we found.**

This is the most important fact about the dunnhumby source, and it constrains
everything else.

`transaction_data.csv` names 2,500 distinct households. `hh_demographic.csv`
names only 801 of them - 32.04%. 1,699 transacting households have no
demographic record at all.

The file is byte-identical (checksum and all) to the copy inside the publisher's
own zip archive, so this is the publisher's coverage and not a truncated
download. It also explains why no foreign key runs from `transactions` to
`households`: one genuinely does not hold.

Any demographic split of this panel is therefore a split of under a third of
the households, and the documented conclusion has to say so.

_1 row(s), 2,842 ms._

| households_transacting | households_with_demographics | households_missing_demographics | pct_with_demographics | pct_of_rfm_households_described |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2500 | 801 | 1699 | 32.04 | 32.04 |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- The headline data-quality finding for this source. transaction_data.csv names
-- 2,500 distinct households; hh_demographic.csv names only 801, and the file
-- is byte-identical to the copy inside the publisher's own zip, so this is the
-- publisher's coverage and not a truncated download. Any demographic split is
-- therefore a minority-sample split and has to be described as one.
SELECT
    (SELECT count(DISTINCT household_key) FROM dunnhumby.transactions)
                                                           AS households_transacting,
    (SELECT count(*) FROM dunnhumby.households)             AS households_with_demographics,
    (SELECT count(DISTINCT t.household_key) FROM dunnhumby.transactions t
       WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM dunnhumby.households h
                         WHERE h.household_key = t.household_key))
                                                           AS households_missing_demographics,
    round(100.0 * (SELECT count(*) FROM dunnhumby.households)
          / (SELECT count(DISTINCT household_key) FROM dunnhumby.transactions), 2)
                                                           AS pct_with_demographics,
    round(100.0 * (SELECT count(*) FROM dunnhumby.households)
          / (SELECT count(*) FROM dunnhumby.household_rfm), 2)
                                                           AS pct_of_rfm_households_described;
```

</details>

### `discount_composition`

Retailer discounts versus manufacturer coupons. Splitting them shows who is actually funding the promotion, which a single discount total cannot.

**What we found.**

Half the panel, 1,282,977 basket lines, carries a retailer discount and nothing
else, at an effective 25.55% of gross. Manufacturer coupons are far rarer:
16,373 coupon-only lines at 31.83%, and 20,049 lines carrying both at 43.48%.

Who pays differs sharply. Where a coupon is involved the manufacturer funds
88.72% of it, but where both apply the manufacturer covers only 36.12%.

The `no discount at all` bucket still shows 8.53 of discount against
1,276,333 lines. That is not a bucketing bug: a handful of lines carry a
POSITIVE `retail_disc` in the raw source, which is why the funding columns take
an absolute value. It is a reminder that this source stores signs two different
ways and that the discount columns must not be trusted without checking.

_4 row(s), 1,546 ms._

| discount_type | basket_lines | gross_sales | discount_given | effective_discount_pct | retailer_funded | manufacturer_funded | pct_funded_by_manufacturer |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. retailer and coupon together | 20049 | 131908.67 | 57354.62 | 43.48 | 31848.09 | 20714.16 | 36.12 |
| 2. retailer discount only | 1282977 | 5348033.40 | 1366495.28 | 25.55 | 1366495.28 | 0.00 | 0.00 |
| 3. manufacturer coupon only | 16373 | 77531.46 | 24680.82 | 31.83 | 0.00 | 21897.38 | 88.72 |
| 4. no discount at all | 1276333 | 3948511.74 | 8.53 | 0.00 | 8.53 | 0.00 | 0.00 |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- Retailer discounts versus manufacturer coupons. Splitting them shows who is
-- actually funding the promotion, which a single discount total cannot.
--
-- SIGN CONVENTION, measured not assumed. This source stores signs two different
-- ways and both are real:
--   * retail_disc / coupon_disc keep the RAW sign: a discount is NEGATIVE.
--     retail_disc is negative on 1,303,026 of 2,595,732 lines (min -180,
--     max +3.99); coupon_disc is negative on 36,422 lines (min -55.93, max 0).
--   * total_discount was normalised during ETL to a POSITIVE magnitude:
--     1,319,391 lines are > 0 (max 180) and only 10 lines are < 0.
-- Bucketing therefore has to test retail_disc/coupon_disc for "< 0", not
-- total_discount for "> 0", or every line lands in "no discount".
SELECT
    CASE
        WHEN retail_disc < 0 AND coupon_disc < 0 THEN '1. retailer and coupon together'
        WHEN retail_disc < 0                     THEN '2. retailer discount only'
        WHEN coupon_disc < 0                     THEN '3. manufacturer coupon only'
        ELSE                                         '4. no discount at all'
    END                                                       AS discount_type,
    count(*)                                                 AS basket_lines,
    round(sum(gross_sales_value), 2)                         AS gross_sales,
    round(abs(sum(total_discount)), 2)                       AS discount_given,
    round(100.0 * abs(sum(total_discount)) / sum(gross_sales_value), 2) AS effective_discount_pct,
    round(abs(sum(retail_disc))::numeric, 2)                 AS retailer_funded,
    round(abs(sum(coupon_disc))::numeric, 2)                 AS manufacturer_funded,
    round(100.0 * abs(sum(coupon_disc)::numeric) / NULLIF(abs(sum(total_discount)), 0), 2)
                                                           AS pct_funded_by_manufacturer
FROM dunnhumby.transactions
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
```

</details>

### `exposure_grid_density`

Why the query above has to restrict. Most of the 36.8 million row exposure grid corresponds to no sale in that product, store and week at all.

**What we found.**

The exposure table is a dense 36,786,524-row product x store x week grid, but
36,302,589 of those rows - 98.68% - correspond to no sale at all. Only 483,935
match a transaction in the same product, store and week.

This is the single most important caveat on any promotion analysis of this
source. The grid is a catalogue of what COULD have been promoted, not a record
of what was, and averaging across it compares 98.68% zeros against 98.68%
zeros.

_1 row(s), 38,551 ms._

| exposure_rows | rows_matching_a_sale | rows_with_no_sale | pct_of_grid_with_no_sale |
|---|---|---|---|
| 36786524 | 483935 | 36302589 | 98.68 |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- Why the query above has to restrict. Most of the 36.8 million row exposure
-- grid corresponds to no sale in that product, store and week at all.
SELECT
    count(*)                                                 AS exposure_rows,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE s.product_id IS NOT NULL)         AS rows_matching_a_sale,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE s.product_id IS NULL)             AS rows_with_no_sale,
    round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE s.product_id IS NULL) / count(*), 2)
                                                           AS pct_of_grid_with_no_sale
FROM dunnhumby.promo_exposure p
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT DISTINCT product_id, store_id, week_no FROM dunnhumby.transactions
) s USING (product_id, store_id, week_no);
```

</details>

### `exposure_vs_sales`

Do products that appear on display actually sell more?

**What we found.**

Restricted to the product-store-weeks that actually sold something, being on
display has no positive association with volume at all: 237,052 on-display
weeks average 1.61 units, while 246,883 off-display weeks average 1.68 units.
Promoted weeks sold slightly LESS.

That is not evidence that promotion suppresses sales. Retailers put products on
display when they already expect them to sell, and the observation here cannot
separate the two. It is enough to say that the display flag on its own does not
predict volume, so any promotion ROI built on this column needs a proper
causal design rather than a comparison.

_2 row(s), 562,888 ms._

| display_status | product_store_weeks_with_sales | avg_weekly_units | total_units | pct_of_all_exposure_rows |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| not on display | 246883 | 1.68 | 413684 | 0.6711 |
| on display | 237052 | 1.61 | 382445 | 0.6444 |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- Do products that appear on display actually sell more?
--
-- Two traps here, both measured rather than guessed. First, promo_exposure is a
-- dense product x store x week grid: 36.8 million rows, and 98.9% of those
-- product-store-weeks have NO matching transaction at all. Comparing averages
-- across the whole grid compares mostly zeros, which says nothing about display.
-- Second, a display comparison over the whole grid also mixes in the fact that
-- retailers promote things they already expect to sell, so any gap is an
-- association and not a causal lift. The query therefore restricts to the
-- product-store-weeks that actually sold, and says so.
WITH sold AS (
    SELECT product_id, store_id, week_no, sum(quantity) AS units
    FROM dunnhumby.transactions
    GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
)
SELECT
    CASE WHEN p.display = '0' THEN 'not on display' ELSE 'on display' END AS display_status,
    count(*)                                                 AS product_store_weeks_with_sales,
    round(avg(s.units), 2)                                   AS avg_weekly_units,
    round(sum(s.units), 0)                                   AS total_units,
    round(100.0 * count(*) / (SELECT count(*) FROM dunnhumby.promo_exposure), 4)
                                                           AS pct_of_all_exposure_rows
FROM dunnhumby.promo_exposure p
JOIN sold s USING (product_id, store_id, week_no)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
```

</details>

### `household_activity_over_time`

How many households actually shopped, week by week? The panel is fixed at 2,500 households, so what moves is participation, not population.

**What we found.**

The panel ramps rather than seasons. Week 1 has 88 households shopping across
142 baskets; by week 50 that is 1,332 households. Gross sales rise with it,
from 6,267.90 in the first week.

Read this as panel onboarding, not demand growth. The first weeks of a retail
panel are always a recruitment artifact, and a trend chart drawn from week 1
would report spectacular growth that is really just households being enrolled.

_102 row(s), 7,142 ms._

| week_no | households_shopping | baskets | basket_lines | avg_units_per_line | gross_sales | net_sales | avg_basket_value |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 88 | 142 | 1881 | 1.25 | 6267.90 | 5211.16 | 44.14 |
| 2 | 175 | 324 | 3675 | 1.97 | 12995.64 | 10821.35 | 40.11 |
| 3 | 228 | 482 | 4803 | 12.03 | 16137.79 | 13498.20 | 33.48 |
| 4 | 270 | 545 | 5379 | 14.29 | 18938.68 | 15965.99 | 34.75 |
| 5 | 370 | 757 | 7168 | 14.19 | 24205.58 | 20139.82 | 31.98 |
| 6 | 433 | 861 | 8896 | 12.52 | 30205.59 | 24923.90 | 35.08 |
| 7 | 491 | 999 | 8980 | 32.01 | 32969.38 | 28073.97 | 33.00 |
| 8 | 530 | 1086 | 10428 | 59.95 | 37644.30 | 31793.77 | 34.66 |
| 9 | 622 | 1212 | 10585 | 79.67 | 37255.33 | 31244.17 | 30.74 |
| 10 | 708 | 1553 | 13543 | 76.09 | 51861.25 | 42994.38 | 33.39 |
| 11 | 846 | 1823 | 16706 | 78.67 | 60051.45 | 51011.30 | 32.94 |
| 12 | 905 | 1926 | 17512 | 70.71 | 63759.38 | 53187.30 | 33.10 |
| 13 | 972 | 2203 | 18634 | 84.58 | 65897.79 | 55203.01 | 29.91 |
| 14 | 1119 | 2433 | 21884 | 72.39 | 76481.74 | 62875.20 | 31.44 |
| _... 36 further rows not shown ..._ | | | | | | | |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- How many households actually shopped, week by week? The panel is fixed at
-- 2,500 households, so what moves is participation, not population.
SELECT
    week_no,
    count(DISTINCT household_key)                            AS households_shopping,
    count(DISTINCT basket_id)                                 AS baskets,
    count(*)                                                  AS basket_lines,
    round(avg(quantity), 2)                                   AS avg_units_per_line,
    round(sum(gross_sales_value), 2)                          AS gross_sales,
    round(sum(sales_value), 2)                                AS net_sales,
    round(sum(gross_sales_value) / NULLIF(count(DISTINCT basket_id), 0), 2)
                                                           AS avg_basket_value
FROM dunnhumby.transactions
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
```

</details>

### `household_participation_rate`

How concentrated is shopping in a few weeks? A panel dataset can look healthy on totals while most households visit only a handful of times all year.

**What we found.**

All 2,500 households in the panel shop at least once, and the average household
makes 110.59 transactions with an average total spend of 3,222.99 across 90.21
active days. The range is enormous: from 1 transaction to 1,300.

The last two columns matter more than the first. Households that have
demographic records average 175.20 transactions, while those without average
80.13 - more than twice as active. Any analysis that restricts to the
described households is not a random sample, it is the most active part of the
panel.

_1 row(s), 41,508 ms._

| households_with_basket | avg_transactions | min_transactions | max_transactions | avg_total_spend | avg_active_days | avg_tx_households_with_demographics | avg_tx_households_without_demographics |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2500 | 110.59 | 1 | 1300 | 3222.99 | 90.21 | 175.20 | 80.13 |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- How concentrated is shopping in a few weeks? A panel dataset can look healthy
-- on totals while most households visit only a handful of times all year.
SELECT
    count(*)                                                  AS households_with_basket,
    round(avg(transactions_per_household), 2)                AS avg_transactions,
    min(transactions_per_household)                           AS min_transactions,
    max(transactions_per_household)                           AS max_transactions,
    round(avg(total_spend), 2)                                AS avg_total_spend,
    round(avg(active_days), 2)                                AS avg_active_days,
    round(avg(transactions_per_household) FILTER (WHERE household_key IN (
            SELECT household_key FROM dunnhumby.households)), 2)
                                                           AS avg_tx_households_with_demographics,
    round(avg(transactions_per_household) FILTER (WHERE household_key NOT IN (
            SELECT household_key FROM dunnhumby.households)), 2)
                                                           AS avg_tx_households_without_demographics
FROM (
    SELECT
        household_key,
        count(DISTINCT basket_id) AS transactions_per_household,
        count(DISTINCT day)      AS active_days,
        sum(sales_value)         AS total_spend
    FROM dunnhumby.transactions
    GROUP BY 1
) h;
```

</details>

### `promo_exposure_coverage`

What share of product-store-weeks were on display or in a mailer. display and mailer are text codes in the source ('0','6','A','D'), not numbers, so they are reported as counts per code rather than summed.

**What we found.**

Display codes are categorical, not numeric - the values here include `0`, `A`
and the digits `1` to `9`, which is why they are counted rather than summed.
Summing this column fails outright with "function sum(text) does not exist".

`0` means no display and covers 21,038,745 product-store-weeks, 57.19% of the
grid. Display exposure of some kind covers the rest, spread thinly across codes
`9` (7.34%), `5` (7.00%), `7` (6.42%), `3` (5.64%) and the remainder. No single
display code reaches even a tenth of the grid.

_10 row(s), 7,849 ms._

| display | product_store_weeks | pct_of_exposure_rows |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 21038745 | 57.19 |
| 9 | 2699467 | 7.34 |
| 5 | 2575289 | 7.00 |
| 7 | 2362118 | 6.42 |
| 3 | 2073738 | 5.64 |
| 6 | 1816021 | 4.94 |
| 2 | 1812840 | 4.93 |
| 1 | 1102141 | 3.00 |
| A | 713180 | 1.94 |
| 4 | 592985 | 1.61 |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- What share of product-store-weeks were on display or in a mailer. display and
-- mailer are text codes in the source ('0','6','A','D'), not numbers, so they
-- are reported as counts per code rather than summed.
SELECT
    display,
    count(*)                                                 AS product_store_weeks,
    round(100.0 * count(*) / sum(count(*)) OVER (), 2)       AS pct_of_exposure_rows
FROM dunnhumby.promo_exposure
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 2 DESC;
```

</details>

### `rfm_segment_value`

The panel's RFM segmentation. Value per household by segment shows which segment actually carries the panel rather than which is largest.

**What we found.**

The largest "segment" in this segmentation is the empty label: 1,699 households,
67.96% of the panel, carrying 3,559,746.82 and 44.18% of panel value.

That is not a segment, it is the absence of one. Those 1,699 households are
exactly the households with no demographic record, because the segment label
comes from the demographic file. The described households are split across
`Level1` to `Level12`, and they are far more valuable: `Level12` averages
10,789.90 per household and `Level9` 8,394.84, against 2,095.20 for the
undescribed group.

So any RFM segment report built on this table silently analyses only the
described minority of the panel while appearing to cover all of it. The segment
has to be treated as missing, not as a category.

_13 row(s), 19 ms._

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
|  | 1699 | 67.96 | 34.12 | 80.13 | 2095.20 | 3559746.82 | 44.18 |
| Level5 | 192 | 7.68 | 6.43 | 167.83 | 5702.35 | 1094852.10 | 13.59 |
| Level4 | 172 | 6.88 | 6.73 | 172.33 | 4802.01 | 825945.47 | 10.25 |
| Level6 | 96 | 3.84 | 9.02 | 149.13 | 5822.53 | 558962.90 | 6.94 |
| Level3 | 77 | 3.08 | 7.73 | 197.84 | 4938.07 | 380231.38 | 4.72 |
| Level1 | 61 | 2.44 | 8.93 | 209.43 | 5559.61 | 339136.30 | 4.21 |
| Level2 | 74 | 2.96 | 8.77 | 164.07 | 4097.12 | 303187.20 | 3.76 |

| Level7 | 34 | 1.36 | 5.88 | 186.56 | 5927.74 | 201543.17 | 2.50 |
| Level12 | 11 | 0.44 | 1.91 | 218.00 | 10789.90 | 118688.90 | 1.47 |
| Level10 | 11 | 0.44 | 1.45 | 190.64 | 8548.46 | 94033.09 | 1.17 |
