<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- The panel's RFM segmentation. Value per household by segment shows which
-- segment actually carries the panel rather than which is largest.
SELECT
    classification_3                                         AS segment,
    count(*)                                                  AS households,
    round(100.0 * count(*) / sum(count(*)) OVER (), 2)       AS pct_of_households,
    round(avg(recency_days), 2)                              AS avg_recency_days,
    round(avg(frequency), 2)                                 AS avg_frequency,
    round(avg(monetary), 2)                                  AS avg_monetary,
    round(sum(monetary), 2)                                  AS total_monetary,
    round(100.0 * sum(monetary) / sum(sum(monetary)) OVER (), 2) AS pct_of_panel_value
FROM dunnhumby.household_rfm
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY total_monetary DESC;
```

</details>

### `sales_mix_by_department`

Which parts of the store carry the business. Department is the top level of the dunnhumby product hierarchy (manufacturer > brand > category > commodity).

**What we found.**

Grocery is half the business: 1,646,076 basket lines and 50.81% of net sales
from 39,019 products. `DRUG GM` follows on 13.10%.

Discount intensity varies far more than volume does. `MEAT` gives away
24.36% of gross and `MEAT-PCKGD` 22.67%, against 17.14% for grocery and 3.07%
for `KIOSK-GAS`. Perishable departments are being promoted harder, which is the
only real signal in this table.

Two rows need care. `KIOSK-GAS` shows 221,254,887 units against 544,222.28 of
net sales, because fuel quantity is recorded in a different unit to everything
else - averaging units across departments mixes incompatible measures. And the
final row, with no department name, carries 10,306.04 of gross fully discounted
to zero net: real rows exist where the department label is missing and the
entire value was given away.

_44 row(s), 8,223 ms._

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| GROCERY | 39019 | 1646076 | 2194762 | 4940586.00 | 4093814.14 | 50.81 | 846771.86 | 17.14 |
| DRUG GM | 31523 | 277232 | 353844 | 1167637.95 | 1055358.03 | 13.10 | 112279.92 | 9.62 |
| PRODUCE | 3117 | 257290 | 319993 | 626356.42 | 557452.11 | 6.92 | 68904.31 | 11.00 |
| MEAT | 2544 | 88416 | 119113 | 725543.29 | 548786.81 | 6.81 | 176756.48 | 24.36 |
| KIOSK-GAS | 16 | 22059 | 221254887 | 561447.72 | 544222.28 | 6.75 | 17225.44 | 3.07 |
| MEAT-PCKGD | 2427 | 111957 | 148148 | 533351.46 | 412436.77 | 5.12 | 120914.69 | 22.67 |
| DELI | 2354 | 62787 | 67026 | 283524.27 | 260866.51 | 3.24 | 22657.76 | 7.99 |
| PASTRY | 2149 | 38179 | 49820 | 139390.00 | 121739.86 | 1.51 | 17650.14 | 12.66 |
| MISC SALES TRAN | 88 | 6050 | 36080860 | 122995.73 | 119960.04 | 1.49 | 3035.69 | 2.47 |
| NUTRITION | 2913 | 32164 | 43253 | 110121.08 | 97669.04 | 1.21 | 12452.04 | 11.31 |
| SEAFOOD-PCKGD | 563 | 11216 | 14003 | 84728.53 | 63093.62 | 0.78 | 21634.91 | 25.53 |
| FLORAL | 938 | 4524 | 5586 | 40853.39 | 39653.34 | 0.49 | 1200.05 | 2.94 |
| COSMETICS | 3007 | 7692 | 7984 | 39669.16 | 32360.37 | 0.40 | 7308.79 | 18.42 |
| SALAD BAR | 48 | 9516 | 10659 | 31834.39 | 30953.30 | 0.38 | 881.09 | 2.77 |
| _... 30 further rows not shown ..._ | | | | | | | | |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- Which parts of the store carry the business. Department is the top level of
-- the dunnhumby product hierarchy (manufacturer > brand > category > commodity).
SELECT
    p.department,
    count(DISTINCT p.product_id)                              AS products,
    count(*)                                                  AS basket_lines,
    round(sum(t.quantity), 0)                                 AS units,
    round(sum(t.gross_sales_value), 2)                        AS gross_sales,
    round(sum(t.sales_value), 2)                              AS net_sales,
    round(100.0 * sum(t.sales_value) / sum(sum(t.sales_value)) OVER (), 2)
                                                           AS pct_of_net_sales,
    round(sum(t.total_discount), 2)                           AS discount_given,
    round(100.0 * sum(t.total_discount) / sum(t.gross_sales_value), 2)
                                                           AS discount_rate_pct
FROM dunnhumby.transactions t
JOIN dunnhumby.products p USING (product_id)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY net_sales DESC;
```

</details>

## M5 - Walmart Global Selling Competition

*Domain: DEMAND FORECASTING. Source file: `backend/sql/m5/01_demand_forecasting.sql`.*

### `demand_scale_by_hierarchy`

How big is each part of the hierarchy? M5 is famously small on the shelf and huge on volume, so item counts and unit counts are reported together.

**What we found.**

M5 is small on the shelf and enormous in volume. `FOODS_3` alone carries 32,937,002
units - 49.21% of everything in the dataset - from 823 items. At the other end
`HOBBIES_2` contributes 541,642 units, 0.81%, from 149 items.

A model evaluated on pooled data will be dominated by `FOODS_3` regardless of
its error, which is the standard argument for scoring these series per
department rather than on a single global mean absolute percentage error.

_7 row(s), 8,912,100 ms._

| dept_id | cat_id | series | items | stores | units | avg_units_per_series_day | pct_of_all_units |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FOODS_3 | FOODS | 8230 | 823 | 10 | 32937002 | 2.06 | 49.21 |
| HOUSEHOLD_1 | HOUSEHOLD | 5320 | 532 | 10 | 11722853 | 1.14 | 17.52 |
| FOODS_2 | FOODS | 3980 | 398 | 10 | 7795025 | 1.01 | 11.65 |
| HOBBIES_1 | HOBBIES | 4160 | 416 | 10 | 5699014 | 0.71 | 8.52 |
| FOODS_1 | FOODS | 2160 | 216 | 10 | 5190400 | 1.24 | 7.76 |
| HOUSEHOLD_2 | HOUSEHOLD | 5150 | 515 | 10 | 3041237 | 0.30 | 4.54 |
| HOBBIES_2 | HOBBIES | 1490 | 149 | 10 | 541642 | 0.19 | 0.81 |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- How big is each part of the hierarchy? M5 is famously small on the shelf and
-- huge on volume, so item counts and unit counts are reported together.
SELECT
    dept_id,
    cat_id,
    count(DISTINCT id)                                        AS series,
    count(DISTINCT item_id)                                   AS items,
    count(DISTINCT store_id)                                  AS stores,
    round(sum(sales), 0)                                      AS units,
    round(avg(sales), 2)                                      AS avg_units_per_series_day,
    round(100.0 * sum(sales) / sum(sum(sales)) OVER (), 2)   AS pct_of_all_units
FROM m5.sales_long
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY units DESC;
```

</details>

### `event_day_impact`

M5's calendar flags holidays (Super Bowl, Christmas, Black Friday). This compares flagged days with ordinary ones, which is the first thing a forecaster needs to know about its own calendar feature.

**What we found.**

Holidays do not lift total demand in this data. The 158 days carrying an event
flag average 33,030 units against 34,609 on the 1,783 ordinary days - a ratio
of 0.96, i.e. event days run BELOW average.

That is counterintuitive for a retail calendar and it is worth stating plainly:
a model that simply adds a "is_holiday" feature will not learn a positive
effect from this data. The real holiday effect in M5 is usually in the product
mix (toys and confectionery before Christmas) rather than in the total, which
is a different query.

_2 row(s), 5 ms._

| event_count | days | avg_units_per_day | vs_average_day |
|---|---|---|---|
| no event flagged | 1783 | 34609 | 1.00 |
| one event | 158 | 33030 | 0.96 |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- M5's calendar flags holidays (Super Bowl, Christmas, Black Friday). This
-- compares flagged days with ordinary ones, which is the first thing a
-- forecaster needs to know about its own calendar feature.
SELECT
    CASE
        WHEN c.event_name_1 IS NULL AND c.event_name_2 IS NULL THEN 'no event flagged'
        WHEN c.event_name_1 IS NOT NULL                       THEN 'one event'
        ELSE                                                        'two events'
    END                                                       AS event_count,
    count(*)                                                  AS days,
    round(avg(t.total_units), 0)                              AS avg_units_per_day,
    round(avg(t.total_units) / (
            SELECT avg(total_units) FROM m5.sales_daily_total), 2)
                                                           AS vs_average_day
FROM m5.sales_daily_total t
JOIN m5.calendar c USING (d_num)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
```

</details>

### `intermittency`

The single most important fact for choosing a forecasting method. M5 series are famously intermittent: most series sell zero on most days, so a mean forecast and a naive "same as yesterday" behave very differently here.

**What we found.**

This is the number that should drive the choice of forecasting method. Of
59,181,090 series-days, 40,241,819 recorded zero units - 68.00%.

The mean is therefore 1.131 units per series-day, but on the 18,939,271 days
that actually sold, the average is 3.534, more than three times higher. The
largest single day in the whole dataset is 763 units.

Any model that predicts a smooth positive number every day will be wrong on
two days in three, and will be systematically wrong in the same direction:
over-predicting on the silent days. Intermittent-demand methods (Croston and
its relatives) or a two-stage classify-then-count design are the appropriate
starting point, and plain exponential smoothing on the level is not.

_1 row(s), 13,196 ms._

| series_days | zero_sales_days | pct_zero_sales_days | avg_units | nonzero_sales_days | avg_units_on_selling_days | max_units_one_day |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 59181090 | 40241819 | 68.00 | 1.131 | 18939271 | 3.534 | 763 |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- The single most important fact for choosing a forecasting method. M5 series
-- are famously intermittent: most series sell zero on most days, so a mean
-- forecast and a naive "same as yesterday" behave very differently here.
SELECT
    count(*)                                                  AS series_days,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE sales = 0)                         AS zero_sales_days,
    round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE sales = 0) / count(*), 2)
                                                           AS pct_zero_sales_days,
    round(avg(sales), 3)                                      AS avg_units,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE sales > 0)                         AS nonzero_sales_days,
    round(avg(sales) FILTER (WHERE sales > 0), 3)             AS avg_units_on_selling_days,
    max(sales)                                                AS max_units_one_day
FROM m5.sales_long;
```

</details>

### `intermittency_by_series`

Intermittency is not uniform across series, and an aggregate percentage hides that. This buckets each series by the share of days it sold nothing. WITH per_series AS (

**What we found.**

Intermittency is not uniform, and an aggregate percentage hides that. 5,133
series (16.84%) fall in the `silent 90%+ of days` band, and between them they
contribute only 838,027 units - 1.25% of all volume. A further 11,591 series
(38.02%) are in `silent 70-89% of days` and carry 10.88% of volume.

At the other end, 4,156 series (13.63%) sell something on most days and
contribute 55.70% of all units.

So a sixth of the series produce about a percent of the demand while a seventh
of them produce over half. Segmenting the panel by intermittency before fitting
anything will matter far more than tuning a single model across all of them.

_4 row(s), 22,922 ms._

| intermittency_band | series | pct_of_series | total_units | pct_of_all_units |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. silent 90%+ of days | 5133 | 16.84 | 838027 | 1.25 |
| 2. silent 70-89% of days | 11591 | 38.02 | 7283331 | 10.88 |
| 3. silent 40-69% of days | 9610 | 31.52 | 21524246 | 32.16 |
| 4. sells something most days | 4156 | 13.63 | 37281569 | 55.70 |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- Intermittency is not uniform across series, and an aggregate percentage hides
-- that. This buckets each series by the share of days it sold nothing.
WITH per_series AS (
    SELECT
        id,
        count(*)                                   AS days,
        count(*) FILTER (WHERE sales = 0)          AS zero_days,
        sum(sales)                                 AS units
    FROM m5.sales_long
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT
    CASE
        WHEN 100.0 * zero_days / days >= 90 THEN '1. silent 90%+ of days'
        WHEN 100.0 * zero_days / days >= 70 THEN '2. silent 70-89% of days'
        WHEN 100.0 * zero_days / days >= 40 THEN '3. silent 40-69% of days'
        WHEN 100.0 * zero_days / days >  0  THEN '4. sells something most days'
        ELSE                                      '5. never zero'
    END                                           AS intermittency_band,
    count(*)                                      AS series,
    round(100.0 * count(*) / sum(count(*)) OVER (), 2) AS pct_of_series,
    round(sum(units), 0)                          AS total_units,
    round(100.0 * sum(units) / sum(sum(units)) OVER (), 2) AS pct_of_all_units
FROM per_series
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
```

</details>

### `price_and_demand`

Does a higher sell price go with lower demand? Prices live in m5.sell_prices per store, item and wm_yr_wk, so the daily facts are first collapsed to the same weekly grain before joining - joining 59 million daily rows to the price table on a daily key that the price table does not have is both wrong and slow. WITH weekly AS (

**What we found.**

Price and volume are strongly inversely related, which is what a cross-category
view of a retailer looks like. Weeks in the `under 1` band average 25.11 units;
`1 to 3`, 13.33; `3 to 5`, 6.74; `5 to 10`, 4.58; and `10 and over`, 3.41.

Two cautions. This is a correlation across different products - cheap staples
sell more than expensive durables because they ARE different products, so it
says nothing about the elasticity of any single item. And the share of weeks
with no sales rises with price too, from 18.74% in the cheapest band to 32.25%
in the dearest, which is a second reason not to read a demand curve into this
table. Per-item price-change analysis is a different query.

_5 row(s), 182,315 ms._

| price_band | item_store_weeks | avg_price | avg_weekly_units | pct_weeks_with_no_sales |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2. under 1 | 470027 | 0.78 | 25.11 | 18.74 |
| 3. 1 to 3 | 2676027 | 2.23 | 13.33 | 20.75 |
| 4. 3 to 5 | 1634942 | 4.14 | 6.74 | 23.30 |
| 5. 5 to 10 | 1546465 | 7.10 | 4.58 | 29.65 |
| 6. 10 and over | 391700 | 14.15 | 3.41 | 32.25 |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- Does a higher sell price go with lower demand? Prices live in m5.sell_prices
-- per store, item and wm_yr_wk, so the daily facts are first collapsed to the
-- same weekly grain before joining - joining 59 million daily rows to the price
-- table on a daily key that the price table does not have is both wrong and slow.
WITH weekly AS (
    SELECT
        s.store_id,
        s.item_id,
        c.wm_yr_wk,
        sum(s.sales) AS units
    FROM m5.sales_long s
    JOIN m5.calendar c USING (d_num)
    GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
),
priced AS (
    SELECT
        w.store_id,
        w.item_id,
        w.wm_yr_wk,
        w.units,
        p.sell_price
    FROM weekly w
    JOIN m5.sell_prices p
      ON p.store_id = w.store_id
     AND p.item_id  = w.item_id
     AND p.wm_yr_wk = w.wm_yr_wk
)
SELECT
    CASE
        WHEN sell_price <= 0        THEN '1. non-positive price'
        WHEN sell_price <  1        THEN '2. under 1'
        WHEN sell_price <  3        THEN '3. 1 to 3'
        WHEN sell_price <  5        THEN '4. 3 to 5'
        WHEN sell_price <  10       THEN '5. 5 to 10'
        ELSE                             '6. 10 and over'
    END                                               AS price_band,
    count(*)                                          AS item_store_weeks,
    round(avg(sell_price), 2)                         AS avg_price,
    round(avg(units), 2)                              AS avg_weekly_units,
    round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE units = 0) / count(*), 2)
                                                      AS pct_weeks_with_no_sales
FROM priced
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
```

</details>

### `store_comparison`

All ten stores carry exactly the same 3,049 series, which makes this a clean like-for-like comparison. CA_3 sells more than double CA_4, so "Walmart demand" is meaningless without naming the store.

**What we found.**

This version of M5 has ten stores, not the three that most write-ups describe.
All of them carry exactly 3,049 series, so the comparison is genuinely
like-for-like and the ranking is about store size rather than about which
products happen to sit in each store.

The spread is large: `CA_3` takes 16.98% of all units while `CA_4` takes 6.25%,
nearly three times less on an identical series list. "Walmart demand" is
meaningless without naming the store, and a forecast trained across all ten
will be dominated by whichever two happen to be busiest.

_10 row(s), 145,450 ms._

| store_id | series | total_units | pct_of_units | avg_units_per_series_day | first_date | last_date |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CA_3 | 3049 | 11363540 | 16.98 | 1.920 | 2011-01-29 00:00:00 | 2016-05-22 00:00:00 |
| CA_1 | 3049 | 7832248 | 11.70 | 1.323 | 2011-01-29 00:00:00 | 2016-05-22 00:00:00 |
| TX_2 | 3049 | 7329642 | 10.95 | 1.239 | 2011-01-29 00:00:00 | 2016-05-22 00:00:00 |
| WI_2 | 3049 | 6697988 | 10.01 | 1.132 | 2011-01-29 00:00:00 | 2016-05-22 00:00:00 |
| WI_3 | 3049 | 6542557 | 9.78 | 1.106 | 2011-01-29 00:00:00 | 2016-05-22 00:00:00 |
| TX_3 | 3049 | 6205940 | 9.27 | 1.049 | 2011-01-29 00:00:00 | 2016-05-22 00:00:00 |
| CA_2 | 3049 | 5818395 | 8.69 | 0.983 | 2011-01-29 00:00:00 | 2016-05-22 00:00:00 |
| TX_1 | 3049 | 5692823 | 8.51 | 0.962 | 2011-01-29 00:00:00 | 2016-05-22 00:00:00 |
| WI_1 | 3049 | 5261506 | 7.86 | 0.889 | 2011-01-29 00:00:00 | 2016-05-22 00:00:00 |
| CA_4 | 3049 | 4182534 | 6.25 | 0.707 | 2011-01-29 00:00:00 | 2016-05-22 00:00:00 |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- All ten stores carry exactly the same 3,049 series, which makes this a clean
-- like-for-like comparison. CA_3 sells more than double CA_4, so "Walmart demand"
-- is meaningless without naming the store.
SELECT
    store_id,
    count(DISTINCT id)                                        AS series,
    round(sum(sales), 0)                                      AS total_units,
    round(100.0 * sum(sales) / sum(sum(sales)) OVER (), 2)   AS pct_of_units,
    round(avg(sales), 3)                                      AS avg_units_per_series_day,
    min(date)                                                 AS first_date,
    max(date)                                                 AS last_date
FROM m5.sales_long
JOIN m5.calendar USING (d_num)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY total_units DESC;
```

</details>

### `weekday_seasonality`

Retail demand is weekly before it is anything else. This is the weekday seasonality a forecaster has to model, measured on the full daily total rather than on a sample. M5 numbers weekdays from 1 = Saturday.

**What we found.**

Saturday is the strongest trading day at 41,706 units averaged, 17.32% of all
volume, with Sunday immediately behind on 41,304. The quietest day is Wednesday
at 30,130, and Thursday at 30,321 is nearly identical.

The Saturday-to-Wednesday gap is roughly a third, which is the single largest
repeatable effect in the data and the first feature any forecaster should
encode. M5 numbers weekdays from 1 = Saturday, not from Monday, so an encoding
that assumes 1 = Monday will be shifted by six days.

_7 row(s), 36 ms._

| wday | weekday | days | avg_units_per_day | min_units | max_units | pct_of_all_units |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Saturday | 278 | 41706 | 25292 | 56340 | 17.32 |
| 2 | Sunday | 278 | 41304 | 13 | 59921 | 17.16 |
| 3 | Monday | 277 | 32995 | 20004 | 47580 | 13.66 |
| 4 | Tuesday | 277 | 30500 | 11 | 44314 | 12.62 |
| 5 | Wednesday | 277 | 30130 | 20 | 43999 | 12.47 |
| 6 | Thursday | 277 | 30321 | 20 | 47028 | 12.55 |
| 7 | Friday | 277 | 34357 | 14 | 54154 | 14.22 |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- Retail demand is weekly before it is anything else. This is the weekday
-- seasonality a forecaster has to model, measured on the full daily total rather
-- than on a sample. M5 numbers weekdays from 1 = Saturday.
SELECT
    c.wday,
    c.weekday,
    count(*)                                                  AS days,
    round(avg(t.total_units), 0)                              AS avg_units_per_day,
    min(t.total_units)                                        AS min_units,
    max(t.total_units)                                        AS max_units,
    round(100.0 * sum(t.total_units) / sum(sum(t.total_units)) OVER (), 2)
                                                           AS pct_of_all_units
FROM m5.sales_daily_total t
JOIN m5.calendar c USING (d_num)
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1;
```

</details>

### `yearly_trend`

How did demand move across the 5.4-year window? Any forecast has to start from the level and direction actually observed, not an assumed trend.

**What we found.**

Total units rise steadily: 8,856,585 in 2011 to 13,800,811 in 2015, with average
daily demand going from 26,281 to 37,810.

2016 shows a higher daily average (41,835) than 2015, which is an artifact and
not an acceleration: it contributes only 143 days of the calendar and ends in
May, so it is a partial year. It is also why the window ends in June rather
than December.

_6 row(s), 4 ms._

| year | days | total_units | avg_units_per_day | avg_saturday_units | avg_sunday_units |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2011 | 337 | 8856585 | 26281 | 23301 | 26732 |
| 2012 | 366 | 12061837 | 32956 | 28957 | 33101 |
| 2013 | 365 | 13135753 | 35988 | 31615 | 36185 |
| 2014 | 365 | 13089776 | 35862 | 31138 | 35456 |
| 2015 | 365 | 13800811 | 37810 | 33536 | 37071 |
| 2016 | 143 | 5982411 | 41835 | 36708 | 40935 |

<details><summary>SQL</summary>

```sql
-- How did demand move across the 5.4-year window? Any forecast has to start
-- from the level and direction actually observed, not an assumed trend.
SELECT
    c.year,
    count(*)                                                  AS days,
    round(sum(t.total_units), 0)                              AS total_units,
    round(avg(t.total_units), 0)                              AS avg_units_per_day,
    round(avg(t.total_units) FILTER (WHERE c.wday = 6), 0)   AS avg_saturday_units,
    round(avg(t.total_units) FILTER (WHERE c.wday = 7), 0)   AS avg_sunday_units
FROM m5.sales_daily_total t
JOIN m5.calendar c USING (d_num)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
```

</details>
